claim: The hippocampal dentate gyrus is an important relay conveying sensory information from the entorhinal cortex to the hippocampus proper.
source: The hippocampal dentate gyrus is an important relay conveying sensory information from the entorhinal cortex to the hippocampus proper.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the anatomical and functional role of the dentate gyrus in the hippocampal circuit.

claim: During exploration, the dentate gyrus has been proposed to act as a pattern separator.
source: During exploration, the dentate gyrus has been proposed to act as a pattern separator.
evidence: This claim references established scientific theory about dentate gyrus function, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The dentate gyrus shows structured activity during immobility and sleep.
source: However, the dentate gyrus also shows structured activity during immobility and sleep.
evidence: This is supported by references to dentate spikes and sharp waves in the introduction section.

claim: In immobile mice, dentate granule cells generate sparse, synchronized activity patterns associated with entorhinal cortex activation.
source: Using dual-color in vivo two-photon Ca2+ imaging, we show that in immobile mice dentate granule cells generate sparse, synchronized activity patterns associated with entorhinal cortex activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from dual-color two-photon imaging experiments.

claim: Dentate gyrus population events during immobility are structured and modified by changes in the environment.
source: These population events are structured and modified by changes in the environment
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing differences between baseline and cue-enriched conditions.

claim: Network events incorporate place- and speed cells.
source: and they incorporate place- and speed cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data identifying place and speed cells and their participation in network events.

claim: Network events during immobility are more similar than expected by chance to population patterns evoked during self-motion.
source: Importantly, they are more similar than expected by chance to population patterns evoked during self-motion.
evidence: This is supported by PCA-based similarity analyses comparing running and network event activity patterns against shuffled controls.

claim: Granule cell activity is required during exploration to form dentate gyrus-dependent spatial memories.
source: Using optogenetic inhibition, we show that granule cell activity is not only required during exploration, but also during immobility in order to form dentate gyrus-dependent spatial memories.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments during the object pattern separation task.

claim: Granule cell activity is required during immobility to form dentate gyrus-dependent spatial memories.
source: Using optogenetic inhibition, we show that granule cell activity is not only required during exploration, but also during immobility in order to form dentate gyrus-dependent spatial memories.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic inhibition experiments showing impaired memory formation when granule cells are inhibited during immobility.

claim: The dentate gyrus receives polymodal sensory information from the entorhinal cortex and relays it into the hippocampal network.
source: The dentate gyrus receives polymodal sensory information from the entorhinal cortex, and relays it into the hippocampal network.
evidence: This is established anatomical and functional knowledge about the dentate gyrus.

claim: Pattern separation requires the animal to generate dissimilar neuronal representations from overlapping input states that represent similar but not identical environments.
source: This capability requires the animal to generate dissimilar neuronal representations from overlapping input states that represent similar but not identical environments (Cayco-Gajic and Silver, 2019).
evidence: This is a definition of pattern separation supported by citation.

claim: Pattern separation has been ascribed to the hippocampal dentate gyrus in species ranging from rodents to humans.
source: Such an operation, termed pattern separation, has been ascribed to the hippocampal dentate gyrus in species ranging from rodents to humans (Berron et al., 2016; Leutgeb et al., 2007; Sakon and Suzuki, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: In the dentate gyrus, polysensory inputs are mapped onto a large number of granule cells which exhibit extremely sparse firing patterns.
source: In the dentate gyrus, polysensory inputs are mapped onto a large number of granule cells which exhibit extremely sparse firing patterns, resulting in a high probability of non-overlapping output patterns (Danielson et al., 2016; GoodSmith et al., 2017; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Pilz et al., 2016; Senzai and Buzsáki, 2017; van Dijk and Fenton, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Sparse firing patterns in dentate gyrus granule cells result in a high probability of non-overlapping output patterns.
source: In the dentate gyrus, polysensory inputs are mapped onto a large number of granule cells which exhibit extremely sparse firing patterns, resulting in a high probability of non-overlapping output patterns (Danielson et al., 2016; GoodSmith et al., 2017; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Pilz et al., 2016; Senzai and Buzsáki, 2017; van Dijk and Fenton, 2018).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the sparse firing patterns, supported by citations.

claim: The dentate gyrus displays prominent electrographic activity patterns such as dentate spikes and sharp waves during immobility or sleep.
source: It displays prominent electrographic activity patterns such as dentate spikes and sharp waves, which occur primarily during immobility or sleep (Bragin et al., 1995; Meier et al., 2020; Penttonen et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: In downstream hippocampal regions such as CA1, neuronal activity during immobility incorporates the replay of behaviorally relevant sequences during sharp wave ripples.
source: In downstream hippocampal regions such as CA1, neuronal activity during immobility incorporates the replay of behaviorally relevant sequences during sharp wave ripples, a process important in memory consolidation (Davidson et al., 2009; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Dupret et al., 2010; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Girardeau et al., 2009; Malvache et al., 2016; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research on CA1 replay.

claim: Replay of behaviorally relevant sequences during sharp wave ripples in CA1 is a process important in memory consolidation.
source: In downstream hippocampal regions such as CA1, neuronal activity during immobility incorporates the replay of behaviorally relevant sequences during sharp wave ripples, a process important in memory consolidation (Davidson et al., 2009; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Dupret et al., 2010; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Girardeau et al., 2009; Malvache et al., 2016; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Little detail is known about how granule cells are active during immobility at the population level in the dentate gyrus.
source: In the dentate gyrus, little detail is known about how granule cells are active during immobility at the population level
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, identifying a gap.

claim: It is unknown whether dentate gyrus activity during immobility reiterates behaviorally relevant information.
source: and it is unknown whether activity during immobility reiterates behaviorally relevant information.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, identifying a gap.

claim: The role of dentate gyrus activity during immobility in memory formation is unclear.
source: Moreover, the role of dentate gyrus activity during immobility in memory formation is unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, identifying a gap.

claim: The firing of dentate granule cells is generally sparse both when animals are immobile and when they are running.
source: As previously described, the firing of GCs was generally sparse (Danielson et al., 2016; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2018; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2012; Pilz et al., 2016), both when animals were immobile and when they were running on a textured belt without additional cues
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and confirmed by the current study's observations.

claim: Mean event frequency of granule cells during immobility is 1.38 ± 0.19 events/min.
source: mean event frequency 1.38 ± 0.19 events/min and 0.97 ± 0.2 events/min, respectively, n = 1415 granule cells in nine mice
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Mean event frequency of granule cells during running is 0.97 ± 0.2 events/min.
source: mean event frequency 1.38 ± 0.19 events/min and 0.97 ± 0.2 events/min, respectively, n = 1415 granule cells in nine mice
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Network events are sparse, incorporating on average only 5.7 ± 0.09% of the total active granule cell population.
source: Network events were sparse, incorporating on average only 5.7 ± 0.09% of the total active GC population.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Network events do not arise by chance.
source: Shuffling analysis (see Materials and methods) confirmed that network events do not arise by chance
evidence: This is supported by shuffling analysis comparing real data to randomized controls.

claim: Network events occurred mainly during immobility periods and were much less prevalent during running.
source: Notably, network events occurred mainly during immobility periods and were much less prevalent during running
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and statistical analysis.

claim: Network event frequencies were significantly higher during immobility (repeated measures ANOVA, F(1,8)=117, p=2×10−6, n = 9 mice, three sessions).
source: Accordingly, network event frequencies were significantly higher during immobility (repeated measures ANOVA, F(1,8)=117, p=2×10−6, n = 9 mice, three sessions, Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: During immobility periods, 99.6% of network events occurred when mice were completely immobile.
source: During immobility periods (defined as running speeds < 4 cm/s), the vast majority of (99.6%) network events occurred when mice were completely immobile.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Network events were on average evenly distributed during the 20 min imaging session.
source: Network events were on average evenly distributed during the 20 min imaging session (Figure 1I)
evidence: This is supported by analysis of the temporal distribution of network events.

claim: Bulk MPP activity was increased during locomotion, consistent with increased sensory input.
source: As expected during exploratory states, the bulk MPP activity was increased during locomotion, consistent with increased sensory input
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations of MPP bulk fluorescence during different behavioral states.

claim: During immobility, larger fluctuations of bulk MPP activity were observed.
source: During immobility in particular, larger fluctuations of bulk MPP activity were observed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and variance analysis.

claim: The variance of the bulk MPP signal was larger during immobility.
source: This phenomenon was reflected in a larger variance of the bulk MPP signal during immobility (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of MPP signal variance.

claim: During immobility, increases in bulk MPP activity were associated with peaks in average granule cell activity levels.
source: Cross-correlation revealed that during immobility, the increases in bulk MPP activity were associated with peaks in average GC activity levels (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by cross-correlation analysis of MPP and GC signals.

claim: Both MPP and GC signals were significantly correlated in most sessions for periods of immobility (8/9 sessions, n = 3 mice, three sessions per mouse, Granger causality test p<0.05).
source: Both signals were significantly correlated in most sessions for periods of immobility (8/9 sessions, n = 3 mice, three sessions per mouse, Granger causality test p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by Granger causality statistical testing.

claim: Aligning GC activity and MPP activity to the timepoint of network events revealed a strong coactivation of GC and MPP during network events.
source: This correlation was clearly visible during network events, because aligning GC activity and MPP activity to the timepoint of network events revealed a strong coactivation of GC and MPP during network events (Figure 2F, n = 3 mice).
evidence: This is supported by temporal alignment analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: During running, MPP signals did not correlate with average GC activity.
source: During running, MPP signals did not correlate with average GC activity, which is not unexpected given the asynchronous activation of GCs during running. 8/9 sessions, Granger causality test p>0.05.
evidence: This is supported by Granger causality testing and is consistent with asynchronous GC activation during running.

claim: Bulk MPP events detected during immobility are on average larger than those detected during running.
source: First, we found that bulk MPP events detected during immobility are on average larger than those detected during running (Figure 2G, Kruskal-Wallis test, n = 3 mice, three sessions per mouse, 8469 and 19,106 events during running and resting, respectively, p=2×10−44)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of MPP event amplitudes.

claim: There were significantly more MPP bulk events during running than during immobility.
source: When we examined the frequencies of all detected MPP bulk events during locomotion and immobility, we found that there were significantly more events during running (repeated measures ANOVA, F(1,2)=255, p=3×10−6, n = 3 mice, three sessions, Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of MPP event frequencies.

claim: Large MPP events (amplitudes above two standard deviations) were significantly more frequent during resting states.
source: However, large events, defined as bulk MPP events with amplitudes above two standard deviations of the mean, were significantly more frequent during resting states (repeated measures ANOVA, F(1,2)=27, p=2×10−3, n = 3 mice, three sessions, Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of large amplitude MPP events.

claim: There was a short temporal delay between individual bulk MPP transients and network events.
source: In line with the correlation of MPP and GC signals, there was a short temporal delay between individual bulk MPP transients and network events (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is supported by temporal analysis shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Pupil diameter is an indicator of neuronal state and arousal.
source: Pupil diameter is an indicator of neuronal state and arousal (Reimer et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2016)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pupil changes can be used to track changes in neuronal states during quiet wakefulness.
source: and can be used to track changes in neuronal states during quiet wakefulness (Reimer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Pupil changes have been shown to closely track the rate of occurrence of hippocampal sharp waves in the CA1 region.
source: Of note, pupil changes have been shown to closely track the rate of occurrence of hippocampal synchronous activity, namely sharp waves in the hippocampal CA1 region (McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Pupil constriction occurs during immobility with dilation at locomotion onsets.
source: As previously described (Reimer et al., 2014; Reimer et al., 2016), we found pupil constriction during immobility with dilation at locomotion onsets (Figure 3B,C, n = 6 mice, three sessions).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations and citations to previous work.

claim: Average pupil diameters during network events were significantly more constricted compared to the average pupil diameters during entire periods of immobility.
source: Intriguingly, the average pupil diameters during network events were significantly more constricted compared to the average pupil diameters during entire periods of immobility (Figure 3D, repeated measures ANOVA for all three groups F(2,28)=17.17, p=1×10−5, n = 6, data from three sessions each, Bonferroni post-tests: pupil diameters during locomotion vs. immobility p=0.0068, locomotion vs. network events p=0.0016, immobility vs. network events p=0.0017).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of pupil diameter measurements.

claim: Network events are specifically associated with pupil constriction.
source: When looking at pupillary dynamics by assessing the rate of diameter change, locomotor episodes were on average associated with pupil dilation, while network events were specifically associated with pupil constriction (Figure 3E, repeated measures ANOVA F(2,28)=34.18, p=3×10−8, n = 6 mice, data from three sessions each, Bonferroni post-tests: pupil diameters during locomotion vs. immobility p=0.0016, locomotion vs. network events p=2.53×10−5, immobility vs. network events p=0.00053).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of pupil diameter change rates.

claim: Network events are associated with specific pupillary dynamics reflecting substates of arousal and neuronal synchronization during immobility.
source: Together, this suggests that network events are associated with specific pupillary dynamics reflecting substates of arousal and neuronal synchronization during immobility.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pupil diameter data and its relationship to network events.

claim: 38% of network event pairs were completely orthogonal to one another.
source: This analysis revealed that 38% of network event pairs were completely orthogonal to one another (Figure 4A, the fraction of completely orthogonal patterns corresponds to the bar with a cosine similarity of zero).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from cosine similarity analysis.

claim: Significantly more orthogonality was observed than expected by chance (38 ± 4% vs. 29 ± 4% in real vs. shuffled data).
source: We found significantly more orthogonality than expected by chance (38 ± 4% vs. 29 ± 4% in real vs. shuffled data, respectively, see Figure 4A inset, n = 9 mice, three sessions, comparison to shuffled data: Wilcoxon test, p=0.0039).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison to shuffled control data.

claim: The observed orthogonality is consistent with the capability to represent separate sets of information within network events.
source: This is consistent with the capability to represent separate sets of information within network events.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the orthogonality analysis.

claim: Specific sub-ensembles of granule cells are repeatedly recruited in network events.
source: To examine if specific sub-ensembles of granule cells are repeatedly recruited in network events, we performed a pairwise Pearson's correlation of the activity of all cell pairs during all network events of a recording session
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis and hierarchical clustering showing repeated activation of cell clusters.

claim: Subgroups of cells are strongly correlated within network event-related activity.
source: This visualization reveals the existence of subgroups of cells that are strongly correlated within network event-related activity (Figure 4C), as previously demonstrated for activity during immobility in the CA1 region (Malvache et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis and comparison to previous work in CA1.

claim: The average cluster size was 6.7 ± 0.4 cells per cluster.
source: Using this definition, the average cluster size was 6.7 ± 0.4 cells per cluster (n = 9 mice, three sessions).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from cluster analysis.

claim: 2.83% of active granule cells exhibited significant place coding.
source: We first identified the group of GCs that exhibited significant place coding (2.83% of n = 1415 active cells imaged in nine mice, Figure 5A for representative polar plots of three GCs).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from place coding analysis.

claim: When calculated as a fraction of only those GCs active during running, the fraction of significantly place-coding GCs was 6.09%.
source: If the fraction of place-coding cells was calculated as a fraction of only those GCs active during running, the fraction of significantly place-coding GCs was 6.09%.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from place coding analysis.

claim: 0.85% of GCs displayed a significant correlation of activity with running speed.
source: Secondly, we identified a fraction of GCs (0.85% of GCs, 1.83% of running-active GCs, n = 9 mice) displaying a significant correlation of activity with running speed (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from speed coding analysis.

claim: The observation of speed-coding granule cells is consistent with data obtained in freely moving mice.
source: This is in contrast to a previous study (Danielson et al., 2016), but consistent with data obtained in freely moving mice (Stefanini et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and comparison to the current findings.

claim: In the cue-enriched condition, the fraction of place cells within the GC population increased to 4.56% of GCs (10.74% of running-active GCs).
source: Under these conditions, the fraction of place cells observed within the GC population increased (4.56% of GCs, 10.74% of running-active GCs)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from place coding analysis in the cue-enriched condition.

claim: In the cue-enriched condition, the proportion of speed cells increased to 1.54% of GCs (3.64% of running-active GCs).
source: as did the proportion of speed cells (1.54% of GCs, 3.64% of running-active GCs, n = 1425 active GCs imaged in nine mice, Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from speed coding analysis in the cue-enriched condition.

claim: The average size of individual network events was significantly larger in the cue-enriched condition compared to the baseline condition.
source: However, the average size of individual network events, measured as the number of participating GCs, was significantly larger in the cue-enriched condition compared to the baseline condition (Figure 6A, Kruskal-Wallis test, n = 9 mice, 1313 and 1493 network events in baseline and cue-enriched condition, respectively, p=4×10−41)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis comparing network event sizes between conditions.

claim: Individual GCs contributed more frequently to network events in the cue-rich condition.
source: with individual GCs contributing more frequently to network events in the cue-rich condition (Figure 6B, Kruskal-Wallis test, p=1×10−40).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of GC participation frequency.

claim: The probability of individual place cells being incorporated in network events was significantly higher in cue-enriched conditions (55.42 vs. 88.46% of place cells in baseline vs. cue-rich conditions).
source: However, when we calculated the fraction of all place cells that participated in network events, taking into account the total number of place cells under each condition, the probability of being incorporated in network events was increased significantly (Figure 6C, 55.42 vs. 88.46% of place cells in baseline vs. cue-rich conditions).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of place cell participation in network events.

claim: The probability of speed cells being incorporated in network events did not change significantly between baseline and cue-rich conditions (42.86 vs. 52.63%).
source: This was not the case for speed cells (42.86 vs. 52.63% of speed cells in baseline vs. cue-rich conditions, n = 9 mice, chi2 test regarding changes in the incorporation of place and speed cells in network events p=3×10−4, post-test: place cells baseline vs. cue-enriched p=1×10−5, indicated with asterisk in Figure 6C, speed cells baseline vs. cue-enriched p=0.22).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of speed cell participation in network events.

claim: The proportion of synchronous events that incorporated at least one place cell increased from 23 ± 9 to 33 ± 11% in cue-enriched conditions.
source: Accordingly, the proportion of synchronous events that incorporated at least one place cell increased (from 23 ± 9 to 33 ± 11%).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from analysis of place cell incorporation in network events.

claim: Significantly more correlated cell clusters contained place cells in the cue-rich condition.
source: but significantly more of the clusters contained place cells in the cue-rich condition (Figure 6D, n = 9 mice, Chi2 test p=0.004, post-test comparison baseline vs. cue-enriched for place cells p=0.004, speed cells p=0.6)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of cluster composition.

claim: Network events are responsive to changes in the environment.
source: Thus, network events are responsive to changes in the environment, and incorporate more place-coding neurons into correlated activity patterns.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differences observed between baseline and cue-enriched conditions.

claim: Network events incorporate more place-coding neurons into correlated activity patterns in cue-enriched environments.
source: Thus, network events are responsive to changes in the environment, and incorporate more place-coding neurons into correlated activity patterns.
evidence: This is supported by the increased incorporation of place cells in network events in cue-enriched conditions.

claim: The dentate gyrus exhibits high lap-to-lap variability in population activity during linear track locomotion.
source: We observed smooth, large trajectories with high variability reflecting movement along the linear track for some laps on the linear treadmill. Such large trajectories did not occur for every lap.
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis of population activity across laps.

claim: CA1 neurons show much lower lap-to-lap variability and relate smoothly to position on the linear track.
source: Here, PCA trajectories showed a much lower lap-to-lap variability and related smoothly to the position on the linear track (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F, for PCA, GPFA, ICA, see Materials and methods, and Figure 7—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis of CA1 population activity.

claim: The population behavior in DG was similar across three different types of linear track, with an episodic nature that was clearly distinct from the repetitive, stable population dynamics in CA1.
source: Thus, the population behavior in DG was similar across three different types of linear track, with an episodic nature that was clearly distinct from the repetitive, stable population dynamics in CA1.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of PCA analyses across different track types and brain regions.

claim: At the population level, network events and locomotion-related activity are more similar than expected by chance.
source: Collectively, these data show that at the population level, NEs and locomotion-related activity are more similar than expected by chance.
evidence: This is supported by multiple PCA-based similarity measures compared to shuffled controls.

claim: The cellular composition of network events matters for the similarity between network events and locomotion-related activity.
source: Moreover, the two shuffling procedures described in Figure 7J and K suggest that the cellular composition of network events matters for this similarity.
evidence: This is supported by shuffling analyses that randomize network event composition.

claim: Inhibiting granule cells during immobility in the learning trial led to a complete loss of preference for the displaced object in subsequent recall trials.
source: This manipulation led to a complete loss of preference for the displaced object in the subsequent recall trials (Figure 8H for representative sessions, analysis of discrimination index in I, unpaired T-test with Welch's correction, n = 6 and 9 for eNpHR and eYFP respectively, t(12) = 5.37, p=0.0002)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the object pattern separation task with optogenetic inhibition.

claim: Control mice displayed a clear preference for the displaced object.
source: whereas control mice displayed a clear preference for the displaced object (Figure 8G for representative session).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from control animals in the object pattern separation task.

claim: Inhibiting granule cell activity when mice actively explored the environment to be memorized led to a loss of preference for the displaced object in subsequent recall trials.
source: As expected, inhibiting GC activity when mice actively explored the environment to be memorized led to a loss of preference for the displaced object in the subsequent recall trials (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from optogenetic inhibition during locomotion.

claim: Network events were associated with pupil constriction and on average smaller pupil diameters when compared to entire periods of immobility, indicating that they may be associated with fluctuations in brain state during immobility.
source: Interestingly, network events were associated with pupil constriction and on average smaller pupil diameters when compared to entire periods of immobility, indicating that they may be associated with fluctuations in brain state during immobility, as described for visual cortex (Reimer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from pupil diameter measurements and comparison to previous work.

claim: The association of pupil constriction with synchronized activity is consistent with data from visual cortex, where brief episodes of pupil constriction during immobility are associated with synchronization and increased low-frequency oscillations.
source: The association of pupil constriction with synchronized activity is also very consistent with data from visual cortex, where brief episodes of pupil constriction during immobility are associated with synchronization and increased low-frequency oscillations (Reimer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to previous work in visual cortex.

claim: For neuronal activity during resting states to support learning or memory consolidation concerning a particular environment, there must be reactivation of activity patterns induced by exploration of the relevant environment.
source: For neuronal activity during resting states to support learning or memory consolidation concerning a particular environment, one general requirement would be that there is reactivation of activity patterns induced by exploration of the relevant environment (Davidson et al., 2009; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Dupret et al., 2010; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Girardeau et al., 2009; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994).
evidence: This is a theoretical requirement supported by citations to previous work on replay and memory consolidation.

claim: Activity during network events is sparse, recruiting just ~5–7% of the active GCs.
source: Indeed, we found that activity during network events is sparse, recruiting just ~5–7% of the active GCs.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: Only ~50% of GCs are active in head-fixed animals.
source: Given that only ~50% of GCs are active in head-fixed animals (Danielson et al., 2016; Pilz et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Recruitment of dentate GCs during network events is much sparser than in other forms of activity occurring during immobility or sleep.
source: recruitment of dentate GCs during network events is much sparser than in other forms of activity occurring during immobility or sleep.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison to other forms of synchronized activity.

claim: The fraction of CA1 neurons recruited during sharp wave ripple mediated replay is much higher than the recruitment of GCs in network events.
source: For instance, the fraction of CA1 neurons recruited during sharp wave ripple mediated replay of behaviorally relevant sequences (Davidson et al., 2009; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007; Dupret et al., 2010; Foster and Wilson, 2006; Girardeau et al., 2009; Malvache et al., 2016; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Wilson and McNaughton, 1994) is much higher than the recruitment of GCs in network events.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison to CA1 replay, supported by citations.

claim: The sparseness of network events predicts that they recruit highly constrained CA3 ensembles.
source: One consequence of the sparseness of network events is that they are predicted to recruit highly constrained CA3 ensembles, both because of the sparse excitatory connectivity of mossy fibers in CA3, and because of the properties of the powerful inhibitory circuits in the CA3 region (Acsády et al., 1998; Neubrandt et al., 2017; Neubrandt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a prediction based on known anatomical and physiological properties of the mossy fiber-CA3 circuit, supported by citations.

claim: Sparse recruitment of CA3 ensembles has been suggested to be important in the capability to store information in CA3, while conserving the pattern separation benefits of the dentate gyrus.
source: This has been suggested to be important in the capability to store information in CA3, while conserving the pattern separation benefits of the dentate gyrus (O'Reilly and McClelland, 1994; GoodSmith et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to computational models and experimental work.

claim: Dentate GC activity may be important to instruct downstream ensembles to exhibit specific memory-related sequences.
source: Thus, dentate activity during immobility may be important to instruct downstream ensembles to exhibit specific memory-related sequences.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed structure of network events and comparison to CA1.

claim: Activity of dentate GCs is necessary for increased SWRs and prospective goal-directed firing of CA3 neurons.
source: That the integrity of the dentate gyrus is important in determining behaviorally relevant firing patterns in CA3 has also been demonstrated by lesion experiments showing that activity of dentate GCs is necessary for increased SWRs and prospective goal-directed firing of CA3 neurons (Sasaki et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to lesion experiments.

claim: The dentate gyrus amplifies small differences between laps and is able to represent successive laps in a different way.
source: One interpretation of this finding is that the dentate gyrus amplifies small difference between laps, and is able to represent successive laps in a different way; this itself being a potential manifestation of the pattern separation capabilities of this structure.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the lap-to-lap variability observed in DG population activity.

claim: The OPS task requires storage of the initial object location with a high degree of precision that can be utilized later on for discriminating the translocated object.
source: The OPS task requires storage of the initial object location with a high degree of precision that can be utilized later on for discriminating the translocated object.
evidence: This is a description of the cognitive demands of the behavioral task used.

claim: Optogenetically inhibiting GCs during immobility remote from the explored objects disrupted the capability to acquire spatial memories in the OPS task.
source: We show that optogenetically inhibiting GCs, even if this was done only during immobility remote from the explored objects, disrupted the capability to acquire such memories.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Dentate network events may rapidly and flexibly introduce information about the environment into the hippocampal network in the time intervals interspersed between episodes of exploration.
source: This supports the idea that dentate network events may rapidly and flexibly introduce information about the environment into the hippocampal network, in the time intervals interspersed between episodes of exploration.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral and imaging data.

claim: Increased incorporation of spatial information via place cell integration into network events was observed upon the first experience of a cue-rich environment.
source: Consistent with this view of 'real-time updating', we observed increased incorporation of spatial information via place cell integration into network events upon the first experience of a cue-rich environment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing baseline and cue-enriched conditions.

claim: Inhibition of the dentate gyrus during the recall phase did not significantly inhibit task performance in the OPS task.
source: Inhibition of the dentate gyrus during the recall phase did not significantly inhibit task performance
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from optogenetic inhibition during recall.

claim: Recall of precise location information is achieved via activation of memory-related attractors in downstream CA3 and/or CA1 regions.
source: consistent with the idea that recall of precise location information is achieved via activation of memory-related attractors in downstream CA3 and/or CA1 regions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data and established knowledge about hippocampal memory circuits.

claim: Behavioral analyses combined with selective lesions of dentate gyrus and CA3 have suggested an interaction between CA3 and DG in supporting encoding but not retrieval processes in a spatial learning task.
source: Indeed, behavioral analyses combined with selective lesions of dentate gyrus and CA3 have also suggested an interaction between CA3 and DG in supporting encoding but not retrieval processes in a spatial learning task (Jerman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous lesion studies.

claim: Disrupting dentate spikes via electrical stimulation has been shown to disrupt acquisition of hippocampal-dependent trace eyeblink conditioning.
source: Moreover, disrupting dentate spikes via electrical stimulation has been shown to disrupt acquisition of hippocampal-dependent trace eyeblink conditioning (Nokia et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous experimental work.

claim: It is possible that the dentate gyrus is encoding the experience of the initial session in the OPS task as a single sequence spanning rest and running.
source: On the other hand, it is possible that the dentate gyrus is encoding the experience of the initial session in the OPS task as a single sequence spanning rest and running.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative interpretation of the behavioral results.

claim: During dentate spikes, granule cells are discharged anterogradely by entorhinal input.
source: During dentate spikes, granule cells are discharged anterogradely by entorhinal input, while they are activated retrogradely by the CA3‐mossy cell feedback pathway during sharp waves (Bragin et al., 1995; Penttonen et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about dentate spike mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: During sharp waves, granule cells are activated retrogradely by the CA3-mossy cell feedback pathway.
source: During dentate spikes, granule cells are discharged anterogradely by entorhinal input, while they are activated retrogradely by the CA3‐mossy cell feedback pathway during sharp waves (Bragin et al., 1995; Penttonen et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge about sharp wave mechanisms, supported by citations.

claim: Dentate network events are associated with MPP activation.
source: We show that dentate network events are associated with MPP activation
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing correlation between MPP and GC activity during network events.

claim: Activity in the dentate gyrus during dentate spikes is associated with wide-spread increases in single-cell activity, gamma oscillations, and intraregional gamma coherence.
source: Along these lines, dentate gyrus activity during dentate spikes is associated with wide-spread increases in single-cell activity, gamma oscillations, and intraregional gamma coherence (Headley et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The precise activation patterns observed in dentate gyrus may be part of a more distributed, organized activity occurring in immobile animals.
source: It is thus possible that the precise activation patterns we observe in dentate gyrus here are part of a more distributed, organized activity occurring in immobile animals.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader context of dentate network events.

claim: Thy1-GCaMP6 (GP4.12Dkim/J) mice express GCaMP6s in most hippocampal neurons.
source: We used 9–12 weeks old Thy1-GCaMP6 mouse line (GP4.12Dkim/J) mice for imaging experiments, which express GCaMP6s in most hippocampal neurons (Dana et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the mouse line used, supported by citation.

claim: Correct injection site in the medial entorhinal cortex was verified in all cases by confined expression of jRGECO1a in the middle molecular layer of the dentate gyrus.
source: Correct injection site in the medial entorhinal cortex was verified in all cases by confined expression of jRGECO1a in the middle molecular layer of the dentate gyrus (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological verification supported by histological analysis.

claim: On average 5–6% of the GC population was active during synchronized network events.
source: On average 5–6% of the GC population was active during synchronized network events (Mean: 5,71%, Median: 5.03%, n = 1312 NEs, nine mice, three sessions).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: No indication of epileptiform activity was observed in Thy1-GCaMP6 (GP4.12Dkim/J) mice.
source: We did not observe any indication of epileptiform activity in Thy1-GCaMP6 (GP4.12Dkim/J) mice, in line with previous work (Steinmetz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data, supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Expression of NpHR was highly selective to the dentate gyrus.
source: Expression of NpHR was highly selective to the dentate gyrus, as described previously (Braganza et al., 2020; Truman et al., 2012), and as reported in the Gensat project (http://www.gensat.org/ShowMMRRCStock.jsp?mmrrc_id=MMRRC:036632).
evidence: This is supported by histological verification and citations to previous work.

claim: Functional evidence has excluded recombination in hilar interneurons in the Prox1-Cre mouse line.
source: Functional evidence has excluded recombination in hilar interneurons in this mouse line (Braganza et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous functional studies.

claim: Crossing the Prox1-Cre mouse line with a mouse leading to Cre-dependent expression of ChR2 showed a lack of monosynaptic inhibitory responses, as would be expected if ChR2 were also present in hilar interneurons.
source: Crossing the Prox1-Cre mouse line used in the present study with a mouse leading to Cre-dependent expression of ChR2 showed a lack of monosynaptic inhibitory responses, as would be expected if ChR2 were also present in hilar interneurons.
evidence: This is functional evidence for the specificity of Cre expression.
